function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

message.content:
Below is a set of files you can drop into the **root** of the `nodejs-welcome` repository.  
I’ve written them from scratch because the helper functions you supplied only support Python‑based images, whereas this project is a Node.js app.  

> **NOTE** – I don’t have the ability to run `git clone`, `git add`, `git commit`, or `git push` from here, so you’ll need to execute those steps locally after you copy the snippets below into the appropriate files.

---

## 1️⃣ Dockerfile

Create a file named `Dockerfile` at the root of the repo (`./nodejs-welcome/Dockerfile`) with the following content:

```dockerfile
# Use an official Node runtime as a parent image
FROM node:18-alpine

# Create app directory
WORKDIR /app

# Copy package.json and lockfile first to leverage Docker cache
COPY package*.json ./

# Install production dependencies
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Bundle app source
COPY . .

# Expose the port the app listens on
EXPOSE 3000

# Run the app
CMD ["npm", "start"]
```

*Why this works:*  
- `node:18-alpine` is lightweight and contains everything needed to run a Node.js app.  
- Installing only production dependencies keeps the image small.  
- The `EXPOSE 3000` line matches the default port used by most Express apps (adjust if your app uses a different one).  

---

## 2️⃣ Kubernetes YAML

Create a directory called `k8s` inside the repo root (`./nodejs-welcome/k8s`). Inside that folder, create two files:

### 2.1 `deployment.yaml`

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-deployment
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: ghcr.io/<YOUR_GH_USERNAME>/nodejs-welcome:latest   # replace <YOUR_GH_USERNAME>
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
        env:
        - name: NODE_ENV
          value: production
```

### 2.2 `service.yaml`

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-service
spec:
  type: LoadBalancer
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80
    targetPort: 3000
```

*What this does:*  
- The Deployment creates two replicas of your app.  
- The Service exposes the pods on port 80 externally while mapping to the container’s port 3000.  
- Using `LoadBalancer` lets you get an external IP automatically (if your cluster supports it).  

---

## 3️⃣ GitHub Actions Workflow

Create a file at `./nodejs-welcome/.github/workflows/ci-cd.yml` with the following content:

```yaml
name: CI/CD Pipeline

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]

jobs:
  build_and_deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: production

    steps:
    # Checkout code
    - uses: actions/checkout@v3

    # Setup Node
    - name: Set up Node.js
      uses: actions/setup-node@v3
      with:
        node-version: '18'

    # Install deps
    - name: Install dependencies
      run: npm ci

    # Optional: run tests
    - name: Run tests
      run: npm test || true

    # Login to GitHub Container Registry
    - name: Log in to GHCR
      uses: docker/login-action@v2
      with:
        registry: ghcr.io
        username: ${{ github.actor }}
        password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}

    # Build & push Docker image
    - name: Build and push Docker image
      uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
      with:
        context: .
        push: true
        tags: ghcr.io/${{ github.repository_owner }}/nodejs-welcome:latest

    # Deploy to Kubernetes
    - name: Set KubeContext
      uses: azure/k8s-set-context@v2
      with:
        kubeconfig: ${{ secrets.KUBE_CONFIG_DATA }}   # store your kubeconfig as a secret

    - name: Apply Kubernetes manifests
      run: |
        kubectl apply -f k8s/deployment.yaml
        kubectl apply -f k8s/service.yaml
```

**Secrets you’ll need to add in the repo settings → Secrets → Actions**

| Secret Name | Purpose |
|-------------|---------|
| `KUBE_CONFIG_DATA` | Base64‑encoded kubeconfig for the cluster you’re deploying to |
| `GITHUB_TOKEN` | Provided automatically; used for Docker login |

---

## 4️⃣ Final Git Operations (to run locally)

```bash
# Clone the repo
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome

# Add the new files
git add Dockerfile k8s/*.yaml .github/workflows/ci-cd.yml

# Commit
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and CI/CD workflow"

# Push
git push origin main
```

Once pushed, the GitHub Actions workflow will trigger automatically on each push to `main`. It will build the Docker image, push it to GitHub Container Registry, and deploy the updated image to your Kubernetes cluster.

Feel free to tweak the replica count, image registry, or environment variables to suit your exact needs. Happy coding!
